title: Async vs sync endpoints
summary: An async def endpoint runs on the event loop: use it when everything it does inside is awaitable.

sections.definition: An async def endpoint runs on the event loop: use it when everything it does inside is awaitable (async driver, httpx). A regular def endpoint is run by FastAPI in a threadpool, so a blocking call does not freeze the server. The only truly bad thing is putting blocking code inside async def. The documentation itself says: if you don't know, use a regular def.
sections.analogy: An async waiter who stands in front of the kitchen waiting for a dish blocks the whole restaurant. If the task is about waiting with no way to get notified, better hire a helper (the threadpool).
sections.problem: With async def and a blocking call, all concurrent requests are served one at a time. Under real load, latency skyrockets.
sections.code:example:
# 1. Bien: librería async dentro de async def
@app.get("/productos/{producto_id}")
async def obtener(producto_id: int, session: AsyncSessionDep):
    return await session.get(Producto, producto_id)

# 2. Bien: librería bloqueante con def (FastAPI usa el threadpool)
@app.get("/tasa-cambio")
def tasa_cambio():
    return requests.get("https://api.banco.co/usd").json()

# 3. Mal: bloqueante dentro de async def
@app.get("/reporte")
async def reporte():
    time.sleep(2)          # nadie más es atendido durante 2 s
    return {"ok": True}
sections.bad:
@app.get("/clientes/{id}")
async def obtener(id: int):
    return psycopg2_buscar(id)   # driver sync en async def

It looks modern and it is the slowest of the three.
sections.good:
@app.get("/clientes/{id}")
def obtener(id: int):
    return psycopg2_buscar(id)   # threadpool

Or you switch to an async driver and use async def with await.
sections.bridge:typescript: In Node everything runs on a single thread: blocking in a handler blocks the entire server, always. FastAPI gives you a way out that Node doesn't have: declare the endpoint with def and let it run on a separate thread.
sections.interview: If inside the endpoint I only use async libraries, I declare it with async def and use await; if I use blocking libraries, I declare it with a regular def and FastAPI runs it in a threadpool. The serious mistake is calling blocking code inside async def, because it freezes the event loop and serializes all requests. For heavy CPU work I use neither: I send it to another process or to a queue.
sections.myths:
• async def with requests, time.sleep or a sync driver.
  • Believing async is always faster.
  • Doing heavy computation inside an endpoint: move it to a process or a task queue.
  • The threadpool is limited (40 threads by default in AnyIO): it is not infinite.

exercises.prompt: Would you declare the endpoint with async def or with def?

items.text: Uses httpx.AsyncClient to query a provider
items.why: Async library: await inside async def.

items.text: Uses requests to query a provider
You don't know whether the library is async
items.why: It is the literal recommendation of the FastAPI docs.
